newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cash crudes steady, sour grades eye Colombia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cash crudes steady, sour grades eye Colombia.

text.p: Cash crude markets in the U.S. Gulf held steady to the end of Wednesday business, finding little impetus to move from established ranges.

Traders said the feature in the market remained Colombia, specifically when shut-in Cano Limon field production would resume. As of late Wednesday, work on repairing the bomb-damaged Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline had not started due to slashing rains and security concerns.

Occidental Petroleum Corp was forced to declare force majeure on Cano production on Tuesday. National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels dynamited the Cano pipeline successfully last week, eventually forcing the line to shut pending repairs.
State-run oil company Ecopetrol estimated Cano Limon had lost two million barrels of output so far this year.

All of the trouble in Colombia helped to keep sour crude prices in the U.S. Gulf strong. Supply concerns allowed West Texas Sour/Midland to trade at a high today $1.12 under WTI/Cushing, later slipping back to $1.15 discounts.
Other grade market discussion late Wednesday saw Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James 22-25 cents more expensive than August WTI/Cushing, even from morning talk.
Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire ranged around a 30 cents discount, the one confirmed price level traded, dealers said.

Midland/WTI failed to excite as well, selling at 21 cents under the WTI/Cushing. The Eugene Island "swamp" grade moved at $1.27 and $1.30 under WTI benchmark, slightly firmer than late Tuesday clockings.
WTI/Cushing Postings Plus stood at $1.88-90, unchanged from Tuesday, and based on the relatively straight August/September roll at minus 10-12 cents.
August Exchange for Physicals (EFPs) remined at even to two cents offered above the paper price, steady from earlier in the week, traders said.

Outright benchmark crude found underlying pressure from late Tuesday reports that Iraq may be forced to immediately sell larger quantities of "oil-for-food" sales than expected, once liftings resume in late July or early August.
According to the U.N. resolution controlling the oil accord, Iraq must sell $2 billion worth of oil in two separate 90-day periods, or $1 billion every 90 days.

Since Iraq has not lifted any "fresh" oil since gaining a six-month extension of the deal from June 8, they must sell the first 90-day ceiling in a shorter timeframe, likely driving volume well above one million barrels per day.
